title: Streams and File I/O
relevance: C++ I/O is library-based (streams, not language syntax), and interviews probe endl vs newline, mixing >> with getline, text vs binary modes, and recovering from failed extraction.

phases.goal: Establish that C++ I/O is a stream abstraction with a class hierarchy and four standard global streams.

must_hit.point: I/O is not built into language syntax; it uses a standard-library stream model: a sequence of characters flowing in or out, decoupling I/O logic from the device.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says streams abstract console/file/string buffers rather than treating I/O as core syntax.

must_hit.point: Hierarchy roots at ios_base (flags/state), then ios (holds streambuf), then istream/ostream (formatted and unformatted I/O); ifstream/istringstream inherit from istream so polymorphism accepts them as istream&.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names ios_base → ios → istream/ostream and notes file/string streams plug in via inheritance.

must_hit.point: <iostream> provides cin (istream), cout (ostream), cerr (unbuffered stderr), and clog (buffered stderr).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four and contrasts cerr immediate vs clog buffered logging.

probes: What is a C++ stream, and how do the standard stream objects and the iostream class hierarchy fit together?

hints.1: Think about whether cin/cout are language keywords or library objects.
hints.2: Sketch ios_base → ios → istream/ostream, then where ifstream sits.
hints.3: Mention cin/cout/cerr/clog and that cerr is unbuffered while clog is buffered.

phases.goal: Explain formatted vs unformatted operations, manipulators, file/string streams, and stream state recovery.

must_hit.point: Formatted >> and << convert between text and binary types; extraction skips leading whitespace. Unformatted I/O (get/read/ignore, put/write, getline) treats raw characters without type conversion or whitespace skipping.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts >> skipping whitespace with get/getline reading raw chars including spaces.

must_hit.point: File streams: ifstream/ofstream/fstream; open modes in/out/app/trunc/binary/ate combinable with |; RAII destructor closes the file when the stream leaves scope; check is_open, operator bool, or fail.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names modes, prefers constructor open + scope exit over manual close, and mentions open-success checks.

must_hit.point: A stream keeps an iostate bitmask: good/eof/fail/bad; failed formatted extraction sets failbit, operator bool becomes false, further I/O is ignored until clear() resets to goodbit, then ignore discards bad buffer data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks fail → clear → ignore after typing non-numeric input into an int extraction.

must_hit.point: String streams: istringstream for parsing/tokenising; ostringstream for building strings; .str() extracts the built string; getline with a custom delimiter tokenises CSV-like input.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows number↔string via ostringstream/istringstream or comma-delimited getline.

probes: How do you open a file, choose text or binary behaviour, and recover after a failed cin >> int extraction?

hints.1: Separate what >> does from what get/read/getline do.
hints.2: Cover fstream open modes, RAII close, then good/fail/clear/ignore.
hints.3: After failbit, clear() then ignore up to newline before retrying input.

phases.goal: Compare buffering, newline strategies, and text versus binary file handling.

must_hit.point: endl writes a newline and flushes; \n only writes a newline—prefer \n in large loops because flushing is a heavy system call unless immediate visibility is required.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States flush difference and performance cost of endl in loops.

must_hit.point: cerr is unbuffered (immediate, good for crash diagnostics); clog is buffered (more efficient for large log volumes).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks cerr for diagnostics and clog for bulk logging based on buffering.

must_hit.point: Default text mode translates line endings (e.g. \r\n on Windows ↔ \n); binary mode with ios::binary leaves bytes untouched—use read/write with a char* buffer for structured/binary data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains newline translation risk and read/write for binary payloads.

probes: What is the difference between std::endl and \n, and when would you open a file in binary mode instead of text mode?

hints.1: Ask what else endl does besides printing a newline.
hints.2: Connect flushing cost to loops; connect text-mode translation to images or raw dumps.
hints.3: endl = newline + flush; binary mode + read/write avoids OS newline translation.

phases.goal: Apply stream patterns to mixed input, file reading, parsing, and safe file lifetime.

must_hit.point: After cin >> value, a trailing newline remains; an immediate getline reads an empty string—discard the leftover with cin.ignore before getline.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes leftover \n and ignore(... max(), '\n') before getline.

must_hit.point: Read files line-by-line with while (getline(fin, line)) and word-by-word with while (fin >> word); use istringstream when asked to parse or tokenise a complex string in memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the two while-loop idioms and names istringstream for in-memory parsing.

must_hit.point: Prefer opening via constructor and relying on RAII destruction over manual close(); Python's with-open safety maps to C++ stream destructors leaving scope.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares Python context managers to C++ file-stream RAII.

probes: Why does getline seem to skip input after cin >> age, and how would you read a file line by line or parse tokens from a string?

hints.1: What character does >> leave in the buffer after reading an integer?
hints.2: Fix with ignore, then contrast getline-loop vs >> loop vs istringstream.
hints.3: ignore leftover newline; while(getline)/while(>>); istringstream for string parsing; RAII closes files.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both emit a newline; endl also flushes. Prefer \n unless you need immediate visibility, because flushing in a large loop is a costly system call.
Both target stderr; cerr is unbuffered for crash diagnostics, clog is buffered and better for large volumes of general log messages.
Text mode performs OS-specific newline translation; binary mode (ios::binary) reads/writes exact bytes. Use unformatted read/write for structured or raw data so translation cannot corrupt it.
Formatted >>/<< convert types and skip leading whitespace on extraction; unformatted get/read/put/write/getline handle raw characters without conversion or whitespace skipping.

tradeoffs.topic: RAII destructor close vs manual close()
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Open via constructor and let the stream leave scope so the destructor closes the handle (RAII), analogous to Python's with open; prefer that over calling close() manually.

gotchas.correction: >> leaves the trailing newline in the buffer; getline consumes it as an empty line. Call ignore to discard through '\n' before getline.

gotchas.trap: Using endl inside a large loop
gotchas.correction: Each endl flushes; prefer \n for newlines and flush only when output must be visible immediately.

gotchas.trap: Reading binary/structured data in default text mode
gotchas.correction: Newline translation can corrupt bytes. Open with ios::binary and transfer with read/write on a char* buffer.

gotchas.trap: Assuming I/O continues after a failed extraction
gotchas.correction: failbit leaves the stream unusable and bad data in the buffer. clear() the state, then ignore the offending input before retrying.

gotchas.trap: Writing structs with write() as portable serialisation
gotchas.correction: Crude struct dumps break with pointers, strings, or cross-system endianness/padding differences.
